SAFIR (PyroGrav) – Spacecraft Atmosphere Fire Intelligence & Risk Platform

SAFIR is an interactive decision-support platform designed to improve fire safety in spacecraft and other reduced-gravity environments. It brings microgravity combustion research and experimental evidence together in one place, helping engineers explore fire risks that may change under different gravity levels, oxygen concentrations, and ventilation conditions.

The platform includes four main modules: a fire-risk prediction and visualization engine, an evidence explorer for comparing research experiments, a cabin smoke-spread and fire-suppression simulator, and a research-gap heatmap that helps identify areas requiring further testing. It also provides uncertainty estimates and a safety lock that flags insufficient evidence instead of presenting an uncertain prediction as safe.

SAFIR addresses the challenge of making decades of space-fire research easier to access, compare, and interpret. It is important because fire incidents in spacecraft can threaten crew safety and mission success. By turning complex research into understandable insights, SAFIR supports better-informed fire-safety decisions and future experimental planning.
details:
SAFIR (PyroGrav) – Spacecraft Atmosphere Fire Intelligence & Risk Platform

Project Description

SAFIR (PyroGrav) is an AI-powered spacecraft fire intelligence and risk assessment platform designed to improve fire safety in space environments, particularly under microgravity, reduced-gravity, and oxygen-enriched cabin conditions.

The platform brings together NASA's ground-based combustion research and microgravity experiments into one integrated workspace. It helps engineers explore research data, compare experiments, predict potential fire hazards, simulate flame and smoke behaviour, and evaluate fire suppression strategies.

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

SAFIR works through four integrated modules:

  • Fire Risk & Live Flame Visualizer: Allows users to adjust gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, ventilation, and material properties to observe changes in flame behaviour and estimate fire risk.
  • Research Evidence Explorer: Organizes 16 flight and ground-test records from research programmes such as NASA ISS FLARE, Saffire I–IV, BASS-II, and ZARM. It ranks similar experiments to help engineers compare evidence under different environmental conditions.
  • Cabin Smoke Simulation: Simulates how smoke travels through a spacecraft cabin, estimates smoke detector alarm times, and compares different fire suppression methods.
  • Research Gap & Experiment Generator: Identifies areas where available evidence is insufficient and generates targeted experiment specifications to guide future research.

The platform uses mathematical physics models, similarity-based evidence retrieval, confidence scoring, and real-time visual simulations to turn complex research information into understandable engineering insights.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Brings multiple space-combustion research records into one accessible platform.
  • Reduces the difficulty of manually searching and comparing research papers and experimental data.
  • Helps engineers understand how gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, and ventilation influence fire behaviour.
  • Provides interactive flame and smoke simulations for different space environments.
  • Compares fire suppression approaches under reduced-gravity conditions.
  • Highlights uncertainty and insufficient evidence instead of presenting unsupported safety conclusions.
  • Generates structured reports and experiment specifications to support engineering decisions.

3. What is the intended impact?

The primary goal of SAFIR is to contribute to safer human spaceflight missions.

Fire behaviour in spacecraft can differ significantly from fire behaviour on Earth because of changes in gravity, airflow, and cabin atmospheric conditions. Understanding these differences is essential for protecting astronauts and spacecraft infrastructure.

SAFIR aims to help aerospace engineers make more informed decisions about fire prevention, detection, containment, and suppression. Its long-term vision is to support fire-safety research and mission preparation for the International Space Station, Artemis Gateway, future lunar missions, Mars habitats, and other human spaceflight environments.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

Software and development technologies:

  • HTML5 Canvas for real-time flame visualisation.
  • JavaScript for interactive calculations and simulation logic.
  • React-based interface architecture.
  • CSS for the aerospace-themed dashboard design.
  • Framer Motion for smooth interface transitions.
  • JSON for research data ingestion, inspection, and export.
  • Node.js and npm for development and dependency management.

Scientific and mathematical methods:

  • Bayesian similarity retrieval.
  • Mahalanobis distance for experimental comparison.
  • Finite-difference modelling for smoke transport.
  • Gravity-adjusted buoyancy calculations.
  • Oxygen enrichment and partial-pressure calculations.
  • Evidence confidence scoring and composite fire-risk assessment.

Development environment: A computer with a modern web browser, Node.js, and npm.

5. How is the project creative and unique?

SAFIR goes beyond being a conventional research database or static dashboard. It combines research discovery, physics-based calculations, interactive visualisation, predictive risk assessment, and smoke simulation in a single workspace.

Its most distinctive feature is its evidence-confidence-based safety mechanism. When the available evidence confidence falls below a defined threshold, the platform automatically classifies the result as INSUFFICIENT EVIDENCE and prevents a low-risk or safe authorisation.

Other unique features include:

  • Interactive comparison of Earth, lunar, Martian, and microgravity flame behaviour.
  • Live adjustment of environmental conditions with immediate visual feedback.
  • Similarity-based matching of historical experiments to new mission conditions.
  • Interactive placement of fire sources and smoke detectors.
  • Comparative evaluation of suppression methods.
  • Automatic generation of targeted research and experiment specifications.

This combination makes SAFIR a research-to-decision platform rather than simply a collection of scientific documents.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, the team considered:

  • Astronaut safety: Prioritising fire prevention, early detection, and reliable mitigation.
  • Microgravity conditions: Accounting for differences in flame shape, buoyancy, and smoke movement.
  • Atmospheric conditions: Considering oxygen concentration, cabin pressure, and ventilation.
  • Scientific reliability: Using experimental evidence and displaying confidence and uncertainty.
  • Research accessibility: Making complex scientific information easier for engineers to find and compare.
  • Simulation usability: Providing interactive visualisations and understandable outputs.
  • Scalability: Designing the platform to accommodate additional experiments, materials, and future mission environments.
  • Safety-first decision-making: Avoiding unsupported safe classifications when sufficient experimental evidence is unavailable.

Overall, SAFIR transforms scattered spacecraft fire research into an interactive intelligence and decision-support platform, helping engineers better understand, evaluate, and prepare for fire hazards beyond Earth.
